The null subspace of measurable functions that vanish almost everywhere
The space $L^p(\mu)$ as the quotient by null functions
Elements of $L^p$ are equivalence classes, so pointwise statements require a representative
$\ell^p$ is the $L^p$ space of counting measure
Holder's inequality for integrals, including the endpoint cases
items.strategy: For 1 < p < infinity, normalize the nonzero norms and apply the published Young inequality pointwise before integrating. Treat the endpoint pairs (1, infinity) and (infinity, 1) separately from the essential-bound definition.

items.title: Equality in Holder's inequality for $1 < p < \infty$
items.strategy: Trace where equality can occur in the normalized Young-inequality proof. Equality in Young forces the normalized powers |f|^p and |g|^q to be proportional almost everywhere, and conversely that proportionality makes the inequality an equality.

items.title: Generalized Holder inequality puts products into $L^r$
items.strategy: Raise |fg| to the r-th power and apply Holder to |f|^r and |g|^r with conjugate exponents p/r and q/r.

items.title: Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for $L^2$
items.strategy: Specialize Holder to p = q = 2, and inherit the equality clause from the strict-exponent equality theorem.

items.title: On a finite counting space, Holder and Cauchy-Schwarz agree with the published finite-dimensional inequalities
Minkowski's inequality for integrals, including $p = \infty$
items.strategy: For 1 < p < infinity, write the p-th power of |f + g| as |f + g| |f + g|^(p - 1) and apply Holder. The cases p = 1 and p = infinity are handled directly from subadditivity of absolute value and the essential-supremum bound.

items.title: Equality in Minkowski's inequality for $1 < p < \infty$
items.strategy: Examine the Holder step in the standard proof of Minkowski. Equality forces the nonnegative functions |f| and |g| to be proportional almost everywhere, and that proportionality is sufficient.

items.title: On a finite counting space, Minkowski agrees with the published finite-dimensional theorem
The essential supremum is attained as the least essential bound
items.strategy: Take the countable family of bad sets {|f| > ||f||_infinity + 1/n}; each is null by minimality of the infimum. Their union is null, giving |f| <= ||f||_infinity almost everywhere, and leastness is built into the definition.

items.title: $\mathcal{L}^p$ and $L^\infty$ are vector spaces for $p \ge 1$
items.strategy: For 1 <= p < infinity, use Minkowski to keep sums in L^p and homogeneity of the integral to keep scalar multiples. For L^infinity, intersect the two essential-bound sets and use countable-union stability of null sets.

items.title: Null functions form a linear subspace and are exactly the zero-seminorm class
items.strategy: Use countable-union stability of null sets for addition and scalar multiplication. For 1 <= p < infinity, the p-seminorm vanishes exactly when the integral of |f|^p is zero; for p = infinity, vanishing means the essential supremum is zero.

items.title: The $L^p$ norm descends to the quotient and makes $L^p$ a normed space for $1 \le p \le \infty$
items.strategy: Use the previous proposition to identify the null functions as the kernel of the seminorm. Hence the seminorm is constant on cosets and separates points on the quotient, while Minkowski and homogeneity descend from representatives.

items.title: Riesz-Fischer completeness of $L^p$ for $1 \le p \le \infty$
items.strategy: For 1 <= p < infinity, choose a rapidly Cauchy subsequence by least indices, sum the successive differences with monotone convergence and Minkowski, and recover the limit by dominated convergence. For p = infinity, union the exceptional null sets and take the pointwise limit outside them.

items.title: $L^p$-convergent sequences have almost-everywhere convergent subsequences
items.strategy: Choose a rapidly convergent subsequence from an L^p-convergent sequence and re-use the subsequence construction inside Riesz-Fischer.

items.title: Convergence in $L^p$ implies convergence in measure
items.strategy: For 1 <= p < infinity, apply Chebyshev-Markov to |f_n - f|^p. For p = infinity, the essential-supremum bound makes the bad set null for all large n.

items.title: On a finite measure space, $L^r$ includes into $L^p$ for $p < r$
items.strategy: Write |f|^p as |f|^p times 1 and apply Holder with exponents r/p and r/(r - p). The finite total measure contributes the factor mu(X)^(1/p - 1/r).

items.title: $\ell^p$ includes into $\ell^r$ for $p < r$
items.strategy: For counting measure, only finitely many terms can exceed 1 when a sequence lies in ell^p. Split the series at that finite set and compare |a_n|^r to |a_n|^p on the tail where |a_n| <= 1.

items.title: Lyapunov's interpolation inequality for $L^p$ norms
items.strategy: If 1/p = theta/p_0 + (1 - theta)/p_1, rewrite |f|^p as the product (|f|^{p_0})^(theta p/p_0) (|f|^{p_1})^((1 - theta) p/p_1) and apply Holder with conjugate exponents 1/theta and 1/(1 - theta).

items.title: Lyapunov interpolation is equivalent to log-convexity of $p \mapsto \log \lVert f \rVert_p$
For essentially bounded $L^r$ functions, the $L^p$ norms converge to the essential supremum
items.strategy: The upper bound is ||f||_p^p <= ||f||_infinity^(p - r) ||f||_r^r. For the lower bound, every epsilon below the essential supremum leaves a set of positive measure where |f| exceeds ||f||_infinity - epsilon, forcing the p-norm above that level as p grows.

items.title: The parallelogram law in $L^2$
items.strategy: Expand |f + g|^2 + |f - g|^2 pointwise to 2|f|^2 + 2|g|^2 and integrate.

items.title: For $0 < p < 1$, the $p$-functional is not a norm
items.strategy: Use the concavity of t maps to t^p on [0, infinity) to show triangle inequality fails on two disjoint equal-mass indicators, so the p-functional is not subadditive and therefore is not a norm.

items.title: For $0 < p < 1$, the $L^p$ distance is a complete translation-invariant metric
items.strategy: Because (a + b)^p <= a^p + b^p for 0 < p < 1, d([f],[g]) = int |f - g|^p dmu defines a metric on quotient classes and is translation invariant. Completeness follows by repeating the Riesz-Fischer telescoping argument without taking p-th roots.

items.title: For $0 < p < 1$, nonnegative functions satisfy the reverse $p$-triangle inequality
items.strategy: For nonnegative numbers a, b and 0 < p < 1 one has (a + b)^p <= a^p + b^p. Apply this pointwise to f and g and then use that (A + B)^(1/p) >= A^(1/p) + B^(1/p) for A, B >= 0.

items.title: A complete normed-space viewpoint on $L^p$ belongs to the later functional-analysis dictionary

title: The $L^p$ Spaces Holder Minkowski and Riesz Fischer — Examples

items.title: The family $x^{-a}$ on $(0,1)$ and $(1,\infty)$ calibrates $L^p$ membership
items.strategy: Integrate x^(-ap) on (0, 1) and on (1, infinity) using the real-power antiderivative and compare the two thresholds ap < 1 and ap > 1.

items.title: The sequence $(k^{-a})$ belongs to $\ell^p$ exactly when $ap > 1$
items.strategy: Apply the real p-series test to the series sum k^(-ap) and read off the threshold ap > 1.

items.title: Finite counting measure on $n$ points recovers the published $p$-norms on $\mathbb{R}^n$
items.strategy: Unwind the counting-measure integral on a finite set and compare it term by term with the published p-norms on R^n.

items.title: The indicator of the rationals has essential supremum $0$ but pointwise supremum $1$
items.strategy: Use that the rationals in [0, 1] are countable and therefore null, so every positive threshold is exceeded only on a null set.

items.title: Proportional functions realize the equality case of Holder
items.strategy: Choose nonnegative functions with |f|^p and |g|^q proportional almost everywhere and invoke the equality theorem.

items.title: A two-step function shows $\lVert f \rVert_p \to \lVert f \rVert_\infty$
items.strategy: Compute the p-norms explicitly for a two-step simple function with two distinct values and let p tend to infinity.

items.title: The parallelogram law on two explicit $L^2$ indicator functions
items.strategy: Evaluate all four L^2 norms on a pair of simple indicator functions and compare the two sides directly.

items.title: $L^1(\mathbb{R})$ is not a subset of $L^2(\mathbb{R})$
items.strategy: Use the power-function family x^(-a) near 0 with 1/2 <= a < 1.

items.title: $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ is not a subset of $L^1(\mathbb{R})$
items.strategy: Use the power-function family x^(-a) at infinity with 1/2 < a <= 1.

items.title: The published typewriter sequence shows why Riesz-Fischer only promises a subsequence
items.strategy: Use the published MT-10 false-statement witness that L^1 convergence need not be almost-everywhere convergence, then combine it with the present page's subsequence corollary to show why the Riesz-Fischer route guarantees only an almost-everywhere convergent subsequence.

items.title: The $p = 1/2$ functional fails the triangle inequality on two indicators
items.strategy: Take two disjoint indicators of equal positive measure. Then the 1/2-functional of the sum exceeds the sum of the two 1/2-functionals.

items.title: A nonzero function on a null set has zero $L^p$ seminorm
items.strategy: Use the indicator of a countable null subset of [0, 1]. It is not the zero function, but its p-seminorm and essential supremum both vanish.

items.title: A Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal{L}^p$ can converge to two distinct functions
items.strategy: Take the constant sequence equal to a nonzero function supported on a null set. Its distance to the zero function is 0, so it converges to both itself and 0 in the pseudometric on calligraphic L^p.

items.title: FALSE: $L^p$ includes into $L^r$ on every measure space whenever $p < r$
items.strategy: Refute with the two power-function counterexamples on the line: one witness lies in L^1 minus L^2 and another lies in L^2 minus L^1.

items.title: FALSE: the $p$-seminorm on $\mathcal{L}^p$ is a norm
items.strategy: Refute with a nonzero function supported on a null set, whose seminorm is 0.

items.title: FALSE: the essential supremum equals the pointwise supremum
items.strategy: Refute with the indicator of the rationals on [0, 1], whose pointwise supremum is 1 but whose essential supremum is 0.

items.title: FALSE: every $L^p$-Cauchy sequence converges pointwise almost everywhere
items.strategy: Refute in L^1 by the published A-page typewriter witness: the sequence converges in norm and therefore is Cauchy, but it has no pointwise limit anywhere on [0,1].

items.title: FALSE: $L^{1/2}$ with its $p$-functional is a normed space
items.strategy: Refute with the explicit 1/2-triangle-inequality failure on two indicators.

items.title: FALSE: equality in Holder forces the functions themselves to be proportional
items.strategy: Refute at the endpoint p = 1, q = infinity with f = 1_A and g = 1 on a proper positive-measure subset A. Equality holds, but the functions are not proportional on the whole space.
